text: Forty years abroad, and the streets of the Rione Sanità still remember who he used to run with. Felice comes back to Naples to sit with his dying mother, an errand meant to be temporary and to end at an airport. Mario Martone keeps him in the quarter instead — its stairwells, its parish, its short sightlines — until leaving would require a decision rather than a ticket. The complication has a name. Oreste was his friend when they were boys in these streets, and now he runs the district's crime; his interest in a returning man is not sentimental. Most of the 117 minutes go to the arithmetic of whether the two will meet, and to a lead performance, honoured with the European Film Award for Best Actor, that carries the whole calculation on one face.

Jeju is small enough that a man's routine can be read by anyone who bothers to watch him keep it. The poet in Kim Yang-hee's film keeps his: the same rooms, the same salt weather, the same lines that cost him nothing to write. Then a boy, and an attention he has no permission to feel and no word for either. The film is careful about that carefulness. It stays with a man being unremarkable in public for most of its 110 minutes and puts the drama in the gaps — a delayed answer, a walk taken by the longer route, a look held one beat past neighbourliness. What unsettles is not secrecy but sincerity: he is not hiding a desire he understands, he is finding out he has one, at a point in life when discovery is an embarrassment.

The daughter is old enough now to want an hour that nobody accounts for, and that is the crisis. Adura Onashile's film sets a young mother and her child in a closeness that has worked until this exact year. Adolescence arrives, the girl reaches for a life that does not report back, and the arrangement that kept them both safe begins to read as confinement. What the mother carries from her earlier life is the engine here, and it stays withheld — not as a trick, but because she has never said it aloud to anyone, least of all to a child she raised to be unafraid. Eighty-seven minutes, no sprawl. The pressure is domestic and constant: shared rooms, shared hours, and a renegotiation neither of them can name while it is happening.

At Coney Island the amusements are somebody's workplace: the carousel needs an operator and the clam house needs a waitress. Woody Allen puts four people inside that arrangement in the 1950s — Ginny, who acted once and now carries plates; Humpty, who runs the ride; a young lifeguard with a play in him; and Humpty's long-estranged daughter, hiding at her father's apartment from gangsters. The register is theatrical on purpose. Speech is heightened, entrances are timed, and Ginny delivers her disappointments as though a house were listening; the effect is of people performing lives too small for the performance. A hundred and one minutes of that friction, between borrowed stage grandeur and four adults who have to be at work in the morning.

The summer of 2015, when a great many people were moving north, and one of them stops at the edge of a Swedish forest. Markus Castro's film declines the report and makes a love story instead. Its Syrian protagonist spends a hundred minutes mostly outdoors, learning one stand of trees the way one learns a language — where the light falls, where the ground gives — and meeting a woman who lives on its border and offers no account of herself. The migration itself stays at the frame's edge, present in what other people assume when they look at him. That is the risk and the interest at once: a film set in the year everyone argued about, which spends its attention on two people among trees and lets the year press in from outside.

A retired opera director hears a mortician sing and concludes that his own stalled career can be revived through another man's throat. That is one quarter of the film. Woody Allen runs four Roman stories in parallel across 111 minutes: an architect watching a young man walk into a mistake he recognises from his own youth, a couple whose afternoon takes each of them somewhere separate, an ordinary citizen who becomes the object of attention nobody explains, and the mortician. Nothing joins them but the city and a refusal to justify any of it — the fame strand in particular proceeds by assertion, a joke that would collapse if anyone asked how. The comedy is broad where Allen's is usually verbal, and Rome absorbs the implausibility without comment.

A glimpse of a face, and a man who had finally decided to settle down starts taking the decision apart. Max is marrying Muriel. Then he sees, or believes he sees, the woman he lost, and Gilles Mimouni turns a romance into a mystery: the object of the search is largely absent from it, and what fills the space is Max's certainty, which grows less trustworthy the more of it he displays. The 116 minutes work by withholding. Each partial answer arrives attached to a further complication, and the pursuit takes on the shape of an investigation run by a man with an interest in the verdict. Muriel, meanwhile, is present, real, and about to marry him; she is the part of this that costs something, and the film knows it.

The overnight run from Tokyo to Niigata is long enough that a man can drive it and think about nothing, provided he is disciplined about it. Riichi Takamiya has been disciplined for years. He lives at the snow end of the route, works while everyone he knows is asleep, and has built a life in which arrivals happen at an hour when nobody is awake to ask questions. Then his ex-wife reappears, at the end of her own resources, just as the younger woman he has been seeing was becoming more than company. Masao Takeshita gives this 157 minutes, which is a decision. The film is not a contest between two women but the long awkward domestic talking that has to be done first, conducted in the hours around a shift by people who are tired.

A transaction she was never party to goes wrong, and the hostage stops being one — which retires, very early, the question of whether she gets out. Luc Besson has 89 minutes and no use for suspense. What replaces it is escalation: the ceiling on what she can do keeps rising, and each new capacity makes the men chasing her more nearly irrelevant, until the pursuit continues on momentum rather than plausibility. It is science fiction in the narrow sense of taking one unfounded premise and following it with a straight face. The pleasure, and it is a real one, lies in watching an action picture give away its own leverage in the first twenty minutes and then move faster rather than slower for the rest.
